headline: The Hedge-Fund Cheat Sheet That Springer Had to Retract
lede: A 361-page compendium by two quant practitioners promises 151 trading strategies "used by hedge funds." The book is real, the math is dense — and Springer has formally retracted it. The strategies, meanwhile, work better before anyone posts them to X.
body:
The PDF being circulated is *151 Trading Strategies*, written by Zura Kakushadze and Juan Andrés Serur and published in 2018 by Palgrave Macmillan, an imprint of Springer Nature. Kakushadze has genuine credentials: a physics Ph.D. from Cornell at twenty-three, postdoctoral work at Harvard, stints at RBC Capital Markets and WorldQuant, and over 130 academic publications spanning physics, finance, and oncology research. The book covers more than 550 mathematical formulas across equity, fixed-income, options, futures, commodities, and foreign-exchange strategies. It is, by any reasonable measure, a serious compendium of documented systematic approaches — not a get-rich pamphlet dressed in LaTeX.

There is a complication. Springer Nature has formally retracted the book, listing it on its platform with the prefix "RETRACTED BOOK." The specific grounds for retraction are not fully disclosed in publicly available materials, though the designation is unambiguous. A preprint version remains freely accessible on SSRN, and third-party sites continue to host the PDF — which is why the document continues to circulate on social media as though it were an untainted resource. Readers encountering this file should note that the publisher has withdrawn its imprimatur, whatever the reason.

The more durable problem with the tweet's framing is the claim that this document "unlocks every algorithm used by hedge funds." It does nothing of the sort — and not merely because the retraction muddies the provenance. The strategies catalogued in the book are **systematic approaches drawn from academic literature and practitioner publications**: momentum, mean-reversion, statistical arbitrage, carry, trend-following, and related factor-based methods. These are not secrets. They appear in the Journal of Finance, in AQR whitepapers, in textbooks used in master's programs from Chicago to London. What hedge funds actually deploy involves layers of proprietary execution logic, risk overlays, bespoke data sources, and continuous recalibration that no published compendium can replicate.

The relevant concept here is *alpha decay* — the tendency for a trading signal's excess return to erode once it is published and capital begins arbitraging it away. R. David McLean and Jeffrey Pontiff documented this rigorously in a 2016 study published in the *Journal of Finance*, examining ninety-seven variables shown to predict cross-sectional stock returns. They found that portfolio returns were, on average, 58% lower after a strategy appeared in an academic paper compared with in-sample estimates. The mechanism is straightforward: publication informs sophisticated investors, who trade on the rule, whose collective pressure drives prices toward efficiency, whose trades progressively eliminate the edge. A compendium of 151 such strategies is, in effect, a catalog of ideas that have already gone through at least one round of that attrition.

This is not to say the book lacks value. For a student of quantitative finance, a compendium of this breadth — spanning volatility strategies, options spreads, commodity seasonality, fixed-income relative value, and equity factor approaches, with accompanying mathematical notation — is a useful map of the territory. It answers the question "what kinds of things have quantitative investors tried?" rather than "what will make money tomorrow?" The distinction matters enormously. Practitioners at established funds spend years on data infrastructure, transaction-cost modeling, and regime detection that transforms an academic idea into a deployable strategy. A 361-page PDF abbreviates all of that into a formula and a brief description.

The tweet's hyperbole is recognizable as a genre: the promise of institutional secrets democratized into a downloadable file. Real alpha, to the extent it persists, lives in proprietary data — satellite imagery of parking lots, credit-card transaction feeds, custom alternative datasets — and in execution advantages that no PDF can convey. What Kakushadze and Serur assembled is a reasonable survey of quantitative methods as they appeared in the academic record through roughly 2018. That the publisher subsequently retracted it adds an irony the tweet does not mention: a book promising to unlock hedge-fund algorithms has itself been quietly locked back up by its own publisher.

concepts.definition: The erosion of a trading signal's excess return over time, particularly after publication or widespread adoption. McLean and Pontiff (2016) found that documented stock-return predictors lose roughly 58% of their in-sample returns once they appear in academic papers, as sophisticated investors trade on the published rule and arbitrage the edge away. Alpha decay is faster for strategies that are easy to implement, highly liquid, and require little proprietary data.

An investment approach in which buy and sell decisions are generated by a defined rule or model rather than by discretionary human judgment. Systematic strategies range from simple momentum rules (buy recent winners, sell recent losers) to complex machine-learning models that combine hundreds of signals. The appeal is consistency and scalability; the vulnerability is that the underlying signals can be identified, published, and arbitraged by competitors.

A style of systematic investing that targets returns associated with specific, repeatable characteristics — such as value (cheap relative to fundamentals), momentum (recent price strength), quality (high profitability), or carry (high yield). Academic research from the 1970s onward documented these patterns; institutional investors have since deployed trillions of dollars chasing them, compressing returns and accelerating the very decay the research predicts.

A class of trading strategies that exploit historically stable statistical relationships between securities — for example, the tendency of two correlated stocks to revert toward their long-run spread after diverging. Unlike pure arbitrage, statistical arbitrage is probabilistic: the relationship can break down permanently, and positions carry real market risk. The strategy is among the most crowded in institutional quantitative trading.

books.title: 151 Trading Strategies
books.author: Zura Kakushadze and Juan Andrés Serur
books.note: The book referenced in the tweet. Published by Palgrave Macmillan/Springer Nature in 2018; formally retracted by the publisher. A preprint version remains on SSRN (abstract_id=3247865). Covers 151 systematic strategies across equities, fixed income, options, futures, commodities, and FX, with more than 550 mathematical formulas. Valuable as a survey of documented methods; should not be mistaken for proprietary hedge-fund algorithms.

books.title: Does Academic Research Destroy Stock Return Predictability?
books.author: R. David McLean and Jeffrey Pontiff
books.note: A landmark 2016 paper in the Journal of Finance examining 97 return predictors. Finds that average returns are 26% lower out-of-sample and 58% lower post-publication, providing the canonical empirical foundation for alpha decay as a concept.

fact_check: The 361-page PDF is confirmed to be *151 Trading Strategies* by Kakushadze and Serur (ISBN 978-3-030-02792-6), published by Palgrave Macmillan in 2018 and available on SSRN (abstract_id=3247865). Springer Nature has formally retracted the book — the publisher's page labels it 'RETRACTED BOOK: 151 Trading Strategies' — though the specific grounds for retraction are not publicly detailed in accessible sources at time of writing. The claim that it unlocks 'every algorithm used by hedge funds' is false: the strategies are drawn from academic literature and practitioner publications, not from proprietary fund code. Kakushadze's credentials (Cornell Ph.D. at 23, Harvard postdoc, WorldQuant Managing Director) are verifiable. The McLean-Pontiff finding that post-publication returns average 58% below in-sample estimates is sourced from their 2016 Journal of Finance paper.
